message.content:
Improve the Nxeon SHARED WEB HOSTING product toward production-readiness — three parts — as CODE-only changes in /opt/nxeon (Next.js + Prisma + Postgres). Do NOT touch any live hosting node, do NOT enable the feature.

Branch `feature/hosting-prodready` off main (main is at 4b525bd). Commit + `git push -u origin feature/hosting-prodready`. Do NOT commit to main, do NOT deploy, do NOT `prisma db push`, do NOT edit .env, do NOT SSH to or change the live hosting node (51.79.226.201), do NOT set ENABLE_SHARED_HOSTING. `npx prisma generate` + `npm run build` MUST pass 0 errors; keep tests passing. PREFER zero schema changes so this phase can promote without a DB migration; if you must add schema, keep it minimal + additive.

=== PART 1 — Provisioner security hardening (worker/hosting.ts) ===
A security review of the live provisioner found these gaps in the per-account PHP-FPM pool + filesystem generation. Fix them in the CODE that GENERATES new-account config (applies to future provisions; do not run anything on the node):
1. CRITICAL — `disable_functions` omits `pcntl_exec` (compiled into PHP → blocklist bypass / open_basedir escape). Add `pcntl_exec` and also `pcntl_fork,pcntl_signal,putenv,mail,dl,proc_nice,symlink,link,error_log,ffi` (and confirm exec,passthru,shell_exec,system,proc_open,popen are present).
2. HIGH — account homes/webroots are `chmod 755` (world-readable → cross-tenant read of wp-config.php if open_basedir is escaped). Change to `750` (or 711 on the home + 750 on webroot) with nginx able to traverse via the account's group, NOT world. Adjust the chown/chmod generation accordingly and document the nginx group approach.
3. Add pool `php_admin_value` limits: `memory_limit` (e.g. 256M), `request_terminate_timeout` (e.g. 120s), and keep `open_basedir` scoped to the home but REMOVE `/tmp` from it (PHP tmp already redirected to the home).
4. MEDIUM — MySQL grant uses a `_`/wildcard-prone pattern: escape `_` and `%` in the DB name for GRANT, and confirm grants are scoped to the exact db (no `*.*`, no FILE/SUPER).
Add/extend unit tests for the pure config-generation helpers (disable_functions contents, perms, grant escaping) in the existing `tsx --test` style. Do NOT change the runtime provisioning flow's external behavior beyond these hardening values.

=== PART 2 — Customer hosting portal improvements ===
The customer-facing hosting control panel (components/customer/HostingClient.tsx + app/dashboard/hosting/*) is currently weak. Review it and improve the UX meaningfully: a clear account overview (domain, plan, status, usage vs quota with a visual bar), well-organized quick actions (file manager, databases, PHP version, WordPress, backups, email), empty/loading/error states, and a "getting started" panel for a freshly provisioned account. Reuse components/ui/primitives.tsx and match the existing portal look. Keep it responsive. Don't invent backend features that don't exist — wire to the existing hosting actions; where an action is not yet available, present it clearly as coming-soon rather than a dead button.

=== PART 3 — Plan recommendations ===
Add a "recommended for" descriptor to each shared-hosting plan, DERIVED FROM the plan's own specs (storage, bandwidth, sites/domains allowed, DB count, etc.). Implement a pure helper lib/hosting/recommend.ts: given a plan's specs, return a short human recommendation like "Recommended for a one-page site with up to ~100 daily visitors" / "Good for a small business site or blog, ~1–2k visits/month" / "Fits a busy WooCommerce store". Derive the tiers sensibly from specs (don't hardcode per-plan). Surface the recommendation on the customer-facing hosting plan cards (the order/pricing UI) and in the admin plan list. Add tests for the helper's tiering. Prefer computing this at render time from existing plan fields (no schema change).

Find the relevant files yourself (grep for HostingPlan, the hosting order/pricing page, admin hosting plan UI, worker/hosting.ts). Reuse conventions (server components, lib/actions-*.ts, requireArea). 

When done: prisma generate + npm run build clean; commit + push the branch; report files changed, whether any schema was added (ideally none), the hardening items applied, build/test result, and the staging command `cd /opt/nxeon && bash scripts/deploy-staging.sh feature/hosting-prodready`. Do not deploy. Do not enable shared hosting.

- figma:figma-code-connect: Creates and maintains Figma Code Connect template files that map Figma components to code snippets. Use when the user mentions Code Connect, Figma component mapping, design-to-code translation, or asks to create/update .figma.ts or .figma.js files.
- figma:figma-create-new-file: **MANDATORY prerequisite** — you MUST invoke this skill BEFORE every `create_new_file` tool call. NEVER call `create_new_file` directly without loading this skill first. Trigger whenever the user wants a new blank Figma file — a new design, FigJam, or Slides file — or when you need a fresh file before calling `use_figma`. Usage — /figma-create-new-file [editorType] [fileName] (e.g. /figma-create-new-file figjam My Whiteboard, /figma-create-new-file slides Q3 Review)
- figma:figma-design-to-code: **MANDATORY prerequisite** — you MUST invoke this skill BEFORE calling the `get_design_context` Figma MCP tool. You MUST trigger this skill whenever the user wants to implement, build, port, or code up a Figma design as code. Example prompts (not exhaustive) are 'implement this Figma design', 'build this screen from Figma', 'turn this Figma into code', 'design to code'. This skill provides critical instructions and steps to the agent on how to correctly implement Figma designs in code and must NOT be skipped.
- figma:figma-generate-design: Use this skill alongside figma-use when the task involves translating an application page, view, or multi-section layout into Figma. Triggers: 'write to Figma', 'create in Figma from code', 'push page to Figma', 'take this app/page and build it in Figma', 'create a screen', 'build a landing page in Figma', 'update the Figma screen to match code', 'convert this modal/dialog/drawer/panel to Figma'. This is the preferred workflow skill whenever the user wants to build or update a full page, modal, dialog, drawer, sidebar, panel, or any composed multi-section view in Figma from code or a description. Discovers design system components, variables, and styles from Code Connect files, existing screens, and library search, then imports them and assembles views incrementally section-by-section using design system tokens instead of hardcoded values.
- figma:figma-generate-diagram: MANDATORY prerequisite — load this skill BEFORE every `generate_diagram` tool call. NEVER call `generate_diagram` directly without loading this skill first. Trigger whenever the user asks to create, generate, draw, render, sketch, or build a diagram — flowchart, architecture diagram, sequence diagram, ERD or entity-relationship diagram, state diagram or state machine, gantt chart, or timeline. Also trigger when the user mentions Mermaid syntax or wants a system architecture, decision tree, dependency graph, API call flow, auth handshake, schema, or pipeline visualized in FigJam. Routes to type-specific guidance, sets universal Mermaid constraints, and tells you when to use a different diagram type or skip the tool entirely (mindmaps, pie charts, class diagrams, etc.).
- figma:figma-generate-library: Build or update a professional-grade design system in Figma from a codebase. Use when the user wants to create variables/tokens, build component libraries, create individual components with proper variant sets and variable bindings, set up theming (light/dark modes), document foundations, or reconcile gaps between code and Figma. Also use when the user asks to create or generate any component in Figma — even a single one — since components require proper variable foundations, variant states, and design token bindings to be production-quality. This skill teaches WHAT to build and in WHAT ORDER — it complements the `figma-use` skill which teaches HOW to call the Plugin API. Both skills should be loaded together.
- figma:figma-implement-motion: Translates Figma motion and animations into production-ready application code. Use when implementing animation/motion from a Figma design — user mentions "implement this motion", "add animation from Figma", "animate this component", provides a Figma URL whose node is animated, or when `get_design_context` returns motion data or instructs you to call `get_motion_context`.
- figma:figma-swiftui: SwiftUI ↔ Figma translation. Use whenever the user mentions Swift, SwiftUI, iOS, iPhone, or iPad — in EITHER direction — translating a Figma design into SwiftUI (design → code), or pushing SwiftUI views / screens / tokens back into a Figma file (code → design). Triggers on phrases like 'implement this Figma design in SwiftUI', 'build this screen in Swift', 'push this SwiftUI view to Figma', 'mirror my Swift code in a Figma file', or whenever a Figma URL appears alongside `.swift` files / an `.xcodeproj`. Routes to a direction-specific reference doc; loads alongside `figma-use` for the code → design path.
- figma:figma-use: **MANDATORY prerequisite** — you MUST invoke this skill BEFORE every `use_figma` tool call. NEVER call `use_figma` directly without loading this skill first. Skipping it causes common, hard-to-debug failures. Trigger whenever the user wants to perform a write action or a unique read action that requires JavaScript execution in the Figma file context — e.g. create/edit/delete nodes, set up variables or tokens, build components and variants, modify auto-layout or fills, bind variables to properties, or inspect file structure programmatically.
- figma:figma-use-figjam: This skill helps agents use Figma's use_figma MCP tool in the FigJam context. Can be used alongside figma-use which has foundational context for using the use_figma tool.
- figma:figma-use-motion: Motion / animation context for the `use_figma` MCP tool — animating Figma nodes via manual keyframes, animation styles, easing, and timeline duration. Load alongside figma-use whenever a task involves adding, editing, or inspecting animation on a node.
- figma:figma-use-slides: This skill helps agents use Figma's use_figma MCP tool in the Slides context. Can be used alongside figma-use which has foundational context for using the use_figma tool.
- anthropic-skills:consolidate-memory: Reflective pass over your memory files — merge duplicates, fix stale facts, prune the index.
- anthropic-skills:docx: Use this skill whenever the user wants to create, read, edit, or manipulate Word documents (.docx files) or Word templates (.dotx files). Triggers include: any mention of 'Word doc', 'word document', '.docx', '.dotx', or requests to produce professional documents with formatting like tables of contents, headings, page numbers, or letterheads. Also use when extracting or reorganizing content from .docx or .dotx files, inserting or replacing images in documents, performing find-and-replace in Word files, working with tracked changes or comments, or converting content into a polished Word document. If the user asks for a 'report', 'memo', 'letter', 'template', or similar deliverable as a Word or .docx file, use this skill. Do NOT use for PDFs, spreadsheets, Google Docs, or general coding tasks unrelated to document generation.
- anthropic-skills:morning: Render the user's morning brief as a styled HTML artifact, or set it up as a recurring weekday task. Use only when the user explicitly asks to run, see, or set up their morning brief, or if they invoke /morning by name. A question about their day, schedule, or calendar is not by itself a request for the brief; answer it directly instead.
- anthropic-skills:pdf: Use this skill whenever the user wants to do anything with PDF files. This includes reading or extracting text/tables from PDFs, combining or merging multiple PDFs into one, splitting PDFs apart, rotating pages, adding watermarks, creating new PDFs, filling PDF forms, encrypting/decrypting PDFs, extracting images, and OCR on scanned PDFs to make them searchable. If the user mentions a .pdf file or asks to produce one, use this skill.
- anthropic-skills:pptx: Use this skill any time a .pptx or .potx file is involved in any way — as input, output, or both. This includes: creating slide decks, pitch decks, or presentations; reading, parsing, or extracting text from any .pptx or .potx file (even if the extracted content will be used elsewhere, like in an email or summary); editing, modifying, or updating existing presentations; combining or splitting slide files; working with templates (.potx), layouts, speaker notes, or comments. Trigger whenever the user mentions "deck," "slides," "presentation," or references a .pptx or .potx filename, regardless of what they plan to do with the content afterward. If a .pptx or .potx file needs to be opened, created, or touched, use this skill.
- anthropic-skills:schedule: Create or update a scheduled task that runs automatically. Use when the user says things like "every day", "each morning", "remind me in an hour", "run this at noon", or wants to reschedule an existing task.
- anthropic-skills:setup-cowork: Guided Cowork setup — install role-matched plugins, connect your tools, try a skill.
- anthropic-skills:skill-creator: Create new skills, modify and improve existing skills, and measure skill performance. Use when users want to create a skill from scratch, edit, or optimize an existing skill, run evals to test a skill, benchmark skill performance with variance analysis, or optimize a skill's description for better triggering accuracy.
- anthropic-skills:xlsx: Use this skill any time a spreadsheet file is the primary input or output. This means any task where the user wants to: open, read, edit, or fix an existing .xlsx, .xlsm, .xltx, .csv, or .tsv file (e.g., adding columns, computing formulas, formatting, charting, cleaning messy data); create a new spreadsheet from scratch or from other data sources; or convert between tabular file formats. Trigger especially when the user references a spreadsheet file by name or path — even casually (like "the xlsx in my downloads") — and wants something done to it or produced from it. Also trigger for cleaning or restructuring messy tabular data files (malformed rows, misplaced headers, junk data) into proper spreadsheets. The deliverable must be a spreadsheet file. Do NOT trigger when the primary deliverable is a Word document, HTML report, standalone Python script, database pipeline, or Google Sheets API integration, even if tabular data is involved.
- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".
- artifact-design: Design guidance and fundamentals for Artifacts.
- artifact-capabilities: Runtime capabilities a published Artifact page can be granted — behavior static HTML cannot provide on its own, such as the page reading live or connected data, keeping state shared across viewers, or updating and republishing itself. Serves this user's live capability roster and the typed call definitions. Load it whenever the user asks for an artifact needing any such runtime behavior.
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo). Omit the interval to let the model self-pace. - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- schedule: Create, update, list, or run scheduled cloud agents (routines) that execute on a cron schedule. - When the user wants to schedule a recurring cloud agent, set up automated tasks, create a cron job for Claude Code, or manage their scheduled agents/routines. Also use when the user wants a one-time scheduled run ("run this once at 3pm", "remind me to check X tomorrow").
- claude-api: Reference for the Claude API / Anthropic SDK — model ids, pricing, params, streaming, tool use, MCP, agents, caching, token counting, model migration.
TRIGGER — read BEFORE opening the target file; don't skip because it "looks like a one-liner" — whenever: the prompt names Claude/Anthropic in any form (Claude, Anthropic, Fable, Opus, Sonnet, Haiku, `anthropic`, `@anthropic-ai`, `claude-*`, `us.anthropic.*`, `[1m]`); the user asks about an LLM (pricing/model choice/limits/caching) — never answer from memory; OR the task is LLM-shaped with provider unstated (agent/MCP/tool-definition/multi-agent/RAG/LLM-judge/computer-use; generate/summarize/extract/classify/rewrite/converse over NL; debugging refusals/cutoffs/streaming/tool-calls/tokens).
SKIP only when another provider is being worked on (overrides all triggers): OpenAI/GPT/Gemini/Llama/Mistral/Cohere/Ollama named in the query; OR `grep -rE 'openai|langchain_openai|google.generativeai|genai|mistralai|cohere|ollama'` over the project hits (run this grep FIRST if no provider named — don't Read the file).
- run: Launch and drive this project's app to see a change working. Use when asked to run, start, or screenshot the app, or to confirm a change works in the real app (not just tests). First looks for a project skill that already covers launching the app; otherwise falls back to built-in patterns per project type (CLI, server, TUI, Electron, browser-driven, library).

content.thinking:
I'm setting up a branch and breaking down the work into parts. First, I need to extract the security-critical config generation helpers from worker/hosting.ts into testable pure functions, then add comprehensive unit tests for the config generation logic including disable_functions contents, permissions, and MySQL grant escaping.

For the disable_functions list, I'm expanding the current set to include pcntl_exec, pcntl_fork, pcntl_signal, putenv, mail, dl, proc_nice, symlink, link, error_log, and ffi while keeping the existing dangerous functions. I'm also planning to refactor the permission handling and MySQL identifier escaping into standalone functions that can be tested without pulling in framework dependencies.

Now I'm working through the permission strategy: home directory should be 711 (root:root) to let nginx traverse without listing, and the webroot should be 750 with ownership set to the user and www-data group so nginx can read and traverse via group membership rather than world permissions.

But there's a complication — the PHP-FPM pool runs as the account user with the account group, so files it creates will be owned by user:accountgroup, not user:www-data. For nginx to read those files via group permissions, either www-data needs to be added to each account's group, or I need to rethink the ownership structure for static files that nginx serves directly. ern is about preventing tenant A's PHP from reading tenant B's wp-config through open_basedir escapes — setting files to 750 instead of 755 blocks tenant B's user and its PHP-FPM pool from accessing tenant A's files since B isn't in group A and isn't world. nginx (www-data) can still read because it's trusted and added to each account's group. The home directory should be 711 owned by root:root so nginx can traverse it to reach the webroot, while tenant B's PHP can traverse but not read tenant A's files.

The fix involves changing home to 711, keeping webroot at 750 with proper ownership, and adding www-data to each tenant's group via usermod — nginx picks up the new group membership on worker respawn, so a full restart isn't strictly necessary but should be documented.

I'm extracting the permission logic into a pure helper function that returns the mode and ownership values, making it testable without side effects. This way I can verify the home directory isn't 755 and webroot is correctly set to 750.

Now I'm moving the FPM pool configuration, MySQL grant SQL builder, and identifier escaping into lib/hosting.ts as pure exported functions so the worker can import and use them. I need to set the PHP memory limit to 256M and configure request timeout limits in the pool settings.

For the open_basedir restriction, I'm removing /tmp from the path since upload_tmp_dir and session.save_path are already scoped to the home directory's tmp folder. The new path will just be the home directory and /usr/share/php.

For MySQL grants, I need to escape underscores and percent signs in the database name since they're treated as wildcards in GRANT statements — without escaping, `nxuser_wp` would match any database like `nxuser<anything>wp`. I'll build the grant statement with properly escaped identifiers to ensure it only applies to the exact database name.

I'm creating a helper function that validates inputs, escapes the wildcards in the database name for the GRANT clause (but not for CREATE DATABASE, which uses the literal name), and returns the complete SQL string for use across the provisioning tasks. Writing SQL generation code... When using wildcards in GRANT statements, MySQL allows `%` and `_` to match database names, and you escape them with backslash to match them literally. Backtick-quoting an identifier in GRANT is tricky because MySQL treats the database name specially in that context, so I should keep the approach robust and match what security requires rather than getting caught up in the nuances of backtick behavior.

I'll refactor the code to write the SQL to a temporary file to avoid shell-quoting complexity, or keep it inline like the existing pattern. The key is to have a helper function that produces just the inner SQL statement without the mysql wrapper, so I can reuse it cleanly.

The simplest approach is to create a pure helper `escapeGrantDbName` that handles the backtick escaping, and a `hostingDbGrantSql` function that returns the canonical SQL fragment for testing. The worker will use these helpers and handle shell escaping of backticks separately. I'll replace the three inline SQL strings with calls to `escapeGrantDbName` for just the GRANT portion. Since the validated inputs only contain safe characters, I just need to escape backticks in the SQL before passing it to the shell: `sql.replace(/`/g, "\\`")`. The backslash-underscore sequences from wildcard escaping will pass through the double-quoted shell literally, so that's fine.

For the refactor, I'm extracting the inline SQL builds into a shared `buildScopedGrantSql` function with backtick escaping, moving the FPM pool config to a pure `buildFpmPoolConfig` helper that takes the user, home, and webroot, and creating a pure `accountFsPlan` helper to return the filesystem permission structure for testability.

Defining the permission plan helper... I'm reconsidering whether a simple reload is enough for www-data to pick up the supplementary group change, or if nginx needs a full restart. Since the task restricts changing runtime behavior beyond the hardening values themselves, I'll document that nginx must be restarted once for the group change to take effect, but leave that to the node onboarding process rather than doing it here.

Actually, there's a cleaner approach: instead of adding www-data to each account group, I could set the webroot group to www-data with chmod 750, so www-data is already the group owner without needing supplementary groups or a restart. But that creates a problem — files created by PHP running as the user would still be owned by that user, and nginx couldn't read newly created static files unless I also set the setgid bit.

The real challenge is that nginx needs to read tenant files, but the tenant user creates those files, and they're in different groups.

The most practical solution is the Hestia-style approach: set the webroot with a setgid directory so new files automatically inherit the www-data group, then nginx reads via group permissions. This works with a reload instead of a restart, and tenant-peer users are blocked by the 750 permissions since they're neither the owner nor in the www-data group. I'll go with home at 711 root:root and webroot owned by www-data. Default umask 022 means PHP-created files end up 644 with www-data group, which is fine since nginx doesn't serve PHP directly and group-readable is safe. Tenant B still can't access anything. So the final permissions setup is: home directory 711 owned by root, webroot 2750 with setgid owned by the tenant user and www-data group, and tmp 700.

Now I'm verifying this actually works—home at 711 means world can traverse but not list, so nginx (as www-data) can reach the webroot through the home directory, and tenant B can traverse home to reach their own webroot but can't list the directory contents.

Next I'll refactor HostingClient.tsx to use the design system primitives. I can show real usage bars for databases (comparing current count against max allowed) and sites, but for disk space I'll display the quota allowance with a note that live usage metering is coming soon rather than inventing a fake bar. This respects the constraint of not fabricating backend data while still delivering the "usage vs quota" visual the task asks for.

I'll compute a capacity score from those specs to derive tiers—Starter for small single-site setups, Basic for small business or blog use, and Business for larger multi-site deployments—each with a descriptive recommendation message.

content.text:
All done. Branch pushed. Summary below.

## Result

Branch `feature/hosting-prodready` (off main @ `4b525bd`) committed as `1a6b65f` and pushed to origin. **No schema changes.** `npx prisma generate` clean, `npm run build` **compiled successfully, 0 errors**. Tests: my new hosting/recommend tests all pass; the 6 failing tests are pre-existing on clean main (verified via stash) and unrelated to hosting. The feature stays gated — `ENABLE_SHARED_HOSTING` untouched, no live node contacted.

### Files changed
- `lib/hosting.ts` — added pure, tested config generators
- `worker/hosting.ts` — consumes the hardened generators (no external-behavior change beyond the hardening values)
- `lib/hosting/recommend.ts` — new pure recommendation helper
- `lib/actions-hosting.ts` — admin plan view now carries `bandwidthTB`
- `components/customer/HostingClient.tsx` — portal rewrite
- `components/admin/HostingInfra.tsx` — "Recommended for" column
- `test/hosting.test.ts`, `test/hosting-recommend.test.ts` — tests

### Part 1 — Provisioner hardening (config-generation only)
1. **CRITICAL** `disable_functions` now includes `pcntl_exec, pcntl_fork, pcntl_signal, putenv, mail, dl, proc_nice, symlink, link, error_log, ffi` on top of the confirmed `exec, passthru, shell_exec, system, proc_open, popen`.
2. **HIGH** webroot no longer world-readable: home `711 root:root` (chroot-safe, nginx can traverse but a peer can't list), webroot `2750 <user>:www-data` (nginx reads via the **www-data group**, setgid keeps tenant-created files in that group; world bits are zero), tmp `700`. Documented in `accountFsPlan`. Restore's fix-perms step re-asserts these.
3. FPM pool adds `memory_limit=256M` and `request_terminate_timeout=120s`; `open_basedir` scoped to the home with **`/tmp` removed** (PHP tmp already redirected into the home).
4. **MEDIUM** MySQL GRANT escapes `_`/`%` in the db name (`escapeGrantDbName`) so a grant can't wildcard onto a neighbour's DB; grants remain db-scoped (`` `db`.* ``, never `*.*`, no FILE/SUPER). All three grant sites (db provision, WordPress, app install) route through the shared `buildScopedGrantSql`.

Unit tests cover disable_functions contents, filesystem perms (asserts no 755/no world bits), open_basedir/limits, and grant escaping.

### Part 2 — Portal (`HostingClient.tsx`)
Account overview (domain link, `StatusDot`, HTTPS badge, plan/PHP), quota tiles with visual bars for databases and sites (real values; live disk metering shown honestly as coming-soon since no backend usage field exists), a "getting started" panel for fresh accounts (install WordPress / point domain / HTTPS), organized quick-actions row, and empty/loading states throughout. Reuses `primitives.tsx`, responsive, all existing action wiring preserved (plus APP_INSTALL result rendering the earlier UI dropped).

### Part 3 — Recommendations (`lib/hosting/recommend.ts`)
`recommendHostingPlan(specs)` derives a tier (starter/personal/business/pro) from a capacity score over disk/sites/DBs/bandwidth — not hardcoded per plan — returning a headline + detail. Surfaced on customer plan cards and the admin plan table. Tiering tests cover boundaries, monotonicity, strong-single-signal promotion, and degenerate specs.

### Staging (not run)
`cd /opt/nxeon && bash scripts/deploy-staging.sh feature/hosting-prodready`

Note: the same 6 pre-existing test failures (login-form state, signup retention, use-server auth surface, webmail MX host, mail ordering) exist on main and are outside this task's scope.
